newsitem.title: FRANCE: UK gelatine still exported despite ban, Lacey says.
newsitem.headline: UK gelatine still exported despite ban, Lacey says.

text.p: A leading researcher into Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) said on Wednesday that Britain was exporting 600,000 tonnes of gelatine a month despite a European Union ban.
"We are exporting infectivity to the rest of the world, still," Professor Richard Lacey told a news conference at the European Parliament.

Lacey said Britain's junior farm minister Angela Browning had told the British parliament last November gelatine exports were continuing and neither government nor industry knew whether the raw materials used came from cows or from other animals.

The EU slapped a ban on all exports of British beef, gelatine, bull semen and embryos last March after the British government revealed there could be a link between bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) and CJD in humans.
The EU-wide ban on gelatine was lifted in June but the decision has never been implemented because uncertainy arose almost immediately about the scientific evidence on which it was based.
"My understanding is there is no gelatine being produced in the UK from British cow sources. All raw materials used are imported," a British government spokeswoman in Strasbourg told Reuters.
Lacey, a professor at Leeds University in northern Britain, said it was not logical for the British gelatine industry to import raw materials.
Countries which could produce the raw materials were much more likely to manufacture the finished product domestically than to ship raw materials to Britain.

Reinhard Schrieber, the head of the Gelatine Manufacturers of Europe, told the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into BSE last November the manufacturers had never asked for an end to the ban on the use of raw materials from countries where there is BSE.
"We know we couldn't market the product because consumers wouldn't buy it," he said.
